extracted.intended_audience: patent applicants, patent attorneys/agents, and patent examiners dealing with AI-related inventions in Japan (JPO) and China (CNIPA)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and examination standards for assessing patent eligibility, novelty/inventive step, sufficiency/enablement, support of claims, and claim drafting for AI-, data-, and software-related inventions before the JPO and the CNIPA.

rubrics_metrics.name: Excluded subject-matter — mental activities (CNIPA Article 25.1(2))
rubrics_metrics.description: The CNIPA lists subject matter excluded from patent protection, including 'rules and methods for mental activities' per Article 25.1(2) CPL.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The CNIPA Guidelines provide a non-exhaustive list of rules/methods regarded as mental activities: mathematical theories and methods of conversion; rules and methods of various games or entertainment; methods of deduction, inference, or operations; methods and systems of managing organization, production, commercial activities or the economy; computer programs per se; and methods of presenting information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'invention' / technical solution requirement (CNIPA Article 2.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Invention' means any new technical solution relating to a product, process or improvement. A technical solution is an aggregation of technical means applying the laws of nature to solve a technical problem; technical means are usually embodied as technical features.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A solution that does not adopt technical means to solve a technical problem and thereby does not achieve any technical effect in compliance with the laws of nature does not constitute an 'invention' under Article 2.2 CPL. Examiners should consider three elements: technical problem, technical means, and technical effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: When an AI-related invention is a 'technical solution' (CNIPA specifics)
rubrics_metrics.description: An AI-related claim counts as a technical solution if: the data processed have exact technical meanings in a technical field and execution of the algorithm directly reflects solving a technical problem under the laws of nature; or the algorithm has specific technical associations with internal computer structure and solves technical problems improving hardware computing efficiency or execution effects; or the solution mines internal associations in big data in a specific application field to improve reliability/accuracy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concrete technical effects include reducing data storage/transmission, improving hardware processing speed, or improving reliability/accuracy of big-data analysis (e.g., classification, clustering, regression, neural networks). See CNIPA Guidelines Section 6.1.2, Chapter 9, Part II.

rubrics_metrics.name: JPO approach for determining statutory 'invention' (two-step style)
rubrics_metrics.description: The JPO assesses whether an AI-related invention constitutes a statutory 'invention' by examining whether the claimed subject-matter expresses information processing based on software/hardware cooperation or is otherwise the creation of technical ideas utilizing laws of nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If it is recognized that a specific information processor or operation method is constructed through cooperation of software and hardware resources, eligibility can be recognized without separately determining whether the intended use is technical. Conversely, if hardware resources that enable information processing for each function are not specifically identified, the JPO may find the claim does not constitute an invention even if it mentions a 'computer'. See the JPO's multi-step process (Step 1/Step 2 referenced).

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical features are crucial for CNIPA eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: In the CNIPA, the presence of 'technical features' is crucial; if no technical features exist, eligibility is denied under Article 25.1 CPL. Also, absence of any of the three elements (technical problem, technical means, technical effect) leads to ineligibility under Article 2(2) CPL.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even where a mathematical model is established using a computer, if it neither improves internal performance of the computer nor causes any technical change in the computer's composition or function, CNIPA may treat it as non-technical and thus ineligible (see Case A-3 comparison).

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty/inventive_step — JPO method
rubrics_metrics.description: The JPO considers claims as a whole (including features not characterized as technical) and selects the most suitable prior art ('primary prior art'), then determines whether a person skilled in the art would easily arrive at the claimed invention by four-step reasoning (see Chapter II.C).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The JPO does not divide claimed features into 'technical' and 'algorithmic' when assessing inventive step; all claimed features are considered in the 'claims as a whole' approach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty/inventive_step — CNIPA method
rubrics_metrics.description: The CNIPA evaluates whether the invention has prominent substantive features and represents notable progress vs prior art, usually following three steps: (1) determine the closest prior art; (2) determine distinguishing features and the technical problem actually solved; (3) determine whether the claimed invention is obvious to a person skilled in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating notable progress, main consideration is whether the invention produces advantageous technical effects. Examiner considerations include motivation to apply other prior art, advantageous effect, and whether there is a technical barrier.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of algorithmic/business features in inventive_step (CNIPA)
rubrics_metrics.description: Algorithmic features or features of rules/methods for business that functionally support and have an interaction relationship with technical features should be considered together with technical features as a whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 'Functionally support each other and have an interaction relationship' means the algorithmic/business features are closely combined with technical features to constitute technical means solving a technical problem and achieving corresponding technical effects; in that case algorithmic features contribute to the technical solution and must be considered in inventive-step analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: JPO vs CNIPA on dividing features for inventive_step
rubrics_metrics.description: Difference: JPO assesses inventive step by considering all claimed features together without dividing them into technical and algorithmic features; CNIPA considers the relationship between algorithmic and technical features and may treat algorithmic features as part of the technical means when closely combined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This makes CNIPA's inventive-step judgment more complex in mixed feature cases; however, if CNIPA treats all claimed subject-matter as technical features, final inventive-step analysis may not significantly differ from JPO practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types that tend to involve an inventive step (both offices)
rubrics_metrics.description: Both JPO and CNIPA tend to find inventive step where: the addition of training data used for learning is not disclosed in reference documents nor common general knowledge; or new AI-related technologies not found in prior art are used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples referenced: Pattern 1 of Claim 2 in Case B-1; Cases B-3 and B-5.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types that tend to lack inventive step (both offices)
rubrics_metrics.description: Both offices tend to find lack of inventive step in cases such as: mere modification of a method for estimating output data based on input data when disclosed in reference documents or common general knowledge; addition of training data that is merely a combination of known data where the technical effect is predictable; and where a skilled person would be motivated to replace the cited AI-related technology with other known AI-related technology and expect the same technical effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Claim 1 in Case B-1; Pattern 2 of Claim 2 in Case B-1; Cases B-2 and B-4.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement requirement — JPO (Article 36(4)(i))
rubrics_metrics.description: The statement (description) shall be clear and sufficient to enable a person ordinarily skilled in the art to work the invention. The JPO determines for each claim whether the skilled person who intends to carry out the claimed invention can understand how to carry it out based on the description, drawings, and common general technical knowledge at filing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A flagged non-enablement situation: a claim to a generic concept where only embodiments of part of the encompassed specific concepts are described such that only those specific concepts can be carried out, and there is a well-founded reason to find other specific concepts are not enabled based on the description plus common general knowledge. Methods of experimentation and analysis may be part of common general technical knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement requirement — CNIPA (Article 26.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: The description shall set forth the invention sufficiently clear and complete so that a person skilled in the art can carry it out, solve the technical problem, and achieve expected technical effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where the description is insufficient, the CNIPA will comprehensively determine whether to accept experimental data submitted by the applicant to overcome the insufficiency, based on the invention disclosure and the content of supplementary experimental data (see Case C-4).

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-filing experimental data: JPO vs CNIPA practice
rubrics_metrics.description: JPO: If the description is insufficient such that a skilled person cannot carry out the invention even in light of common general knowledge at filing, post-filing experimental evidence cannot overcome the insufficiency; applicants can, however, submit written opinions arguing common general knowledge and supporting certificates. CNIPA: may accept experimental data submitted after filing to determine whether the insufficiency has been overcome.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This difference is prominent in practice (Cases C-2, C-3, C-4): JPO is stricter about curing insufficiency with post-filing experiments; CNIPA has a more flexible, case-by-case acceptance of supplementary experimental evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types that satisfy enablement/sufficiency of disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Both offices tend to find enablement/sufficiency where: correlations among multiple types of training data are presumable by common general knowledge; the description contains explanatory/statistical information supporting correlations; or performance evaluation of an actual AI model supports the presence of such correlations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Case C-1 (presumable correlation), Claim 2 in Case C-2 (statistical support), Claim 2 in Case C-3 (performance evaluation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Types that do not satisfy enablement/sufficiency of disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples of non-enablement include: where the description does not support correlations claimed among training data and such correlations cannot be inferred from common general knowledge (JPO cases); claims relying on AI estimates without verification on actual products when such substitution is not common general knowledge; CNIPA: concrete technical solution without experimental evidence when the solution can only be established upon experimental confirmation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific examples: Claim 1 in Case C-2 and Claim 1 in Case C-3 (JPO non-enable); Case C-4 where description needs experimental evidence (CNIPA).

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims supported by the description — JPO (support requirement Article 36(6)(i))
rubrics_metrics.description: A claimed invention shall be disclosed in the description. If the claimed invention exceeds 'the extent of disclosure in the description to which a person skilled in the art would recognize that a problem to be solved would actually be solved', the claims fail the support requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enablement and support are different purposes; violation of one does not necessarily imply violation of the other. However, in AI-related cases, where enablement fails (see types above), it is likely the support requirement will also fail because the claim exceeds the scope described as enableable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims supported by the description — CNIPA (Article 26.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims shall be supported by the description and shall define the extent of patent protection sought clearly and concisely. The technical solution in each claim shall be one that a person skilled in the art can reach directly or by generalization from the sufficiently disclosed contents in the description and shall not go beyond the scope of the contents disclosed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In CNIPA practice, whether claims are supported is generally considered only when the description discloses the invention sufficiently; if the description is insufficient, the issue of claim support may not be separately considered (see Case C-4).

rubrics_metrics.name: Generalization in claims — CNIPA caution
rubrics_metrics.description: For claims generalized in generic terms, examiners shall examine whether the generalization can be supported by the description. Where generalization includes content speculated by the applicant and the effect is difficult to determine or evaluate beforehand, the generalization is regarded as going beyond the contents disclosed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the generalization leads a skilled person to reasonably doubt that one or more specific options included in the generic term can solve the technical problem and achieve the same technical effects, the claim is not supported by the description (examples: Claim 1 in Case C-2, Claim 1 in Case C-3).

rubrics_metrics.name: Eligibility of claims pertaining to data — JPO stance
rubrics_metrics.description: The JPO does not treat 'data' per se as equivalent to a program; what is acceptable is 'data with a structure that has similar properties to a computer program', i.e., data that prescribe the processing performed by the computer ('structured data').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If structured data is recognized as equivalent to a program, it may be evaluated under the 'idea based on the standpoint of software' and more likely qualify as an invention. If data are characterized only by informational content, eligibility is not satisfied. A 'data structure' is an acceptable claim format regardless of storage medium.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eligibility of claims pertaining to data — CNIPA stance
rubrics_metrics.description: In CNIPA practice, a claim titled 'data' that only involves the training data itself (specific numerical values/feature values) and contains no technical features is a method of presenting information (rules/methods for mental activities) and is not patentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If, however, the claim's features include technical features (technical means applying laws of nature producing technical effects), then the claim is a technical solution under Article 2.2 CPL and may be patentable. Thus, the presence of technical features in data-related claims is determinative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity of categories — JPO (data/program/model labeling)
rubrics_metrics.description: Article 2(3) JPA includes computer programs in the term 'product'. If description/drawings and common general technical knowledge make clear the claimed invention is a 'program' even if labeled differently (module/library/neural network/model), it will be handled as a 'program' (invention of a product).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structured data/data structure with features similar to programs (they define computer processing by their structure) are recognized as 'equivalent to computer programs' and handled as product claims. See JPHB Annex B guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity of categories — CNIPA (titles do not determine category)
rubrics_metrics.description: In CNIPA practice, titles like 'data', 'computer program', and 'model' do not by themselves indicate whether the claims are product or process claims; therefore such claims may not comply with the clarity requirement under Article 26.4 CPL.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants should make clear in the description and claims whether the subject-matter is intended as a product claim, process claim, or other category to satisfy clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant guidance — JPO filing practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants filing software-related inventions with the JPO are required to explicitly disclose the invention as 'the creation of technical ideas utilizing the laws of nature' or 'information processing by the software realized using hardware resources concretely' to satisfy eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants may file 'program', 'data structure', or 'model' as subject-matter in the category of an 'invention of a product' if recognized as equivalent to a computer program; explicit disclosure of concrete hardware realization helps secure the product/invention categorization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant guidance — CNIPA filing practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants filing AI-related inventions with the CNIPA should explicitly disclose the invention as 'an aggregation of technical means applying the laws of nature to solve a technical problem'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Filed claims can be process claims (method for ...) or product claims (system for..., apparatus for..., computer-readable storage medium, computer program product). Ensure the description shows technical features/technical effects consistent with Article 2.2 CPL.
